title: Future
Long-life runs: an agent's control over its own lifespan
description:
Findings from a review of the default harness (services/chassis.py, services/supervisor.py, tasks/duty.py) against the requirements of agent runs lasting several hours.

The goal is not endurance alone. It is an agent that can actively stretch its own life as far as that is useful, AND recognise when continuing is worse than starting over. Endurance is the floor; agency over lifespan is the actual target.

Four clusters:

  1. STRETCH -- the levers that make a long run possible. The recap is lossy truncation rather than compaction, and the compaction primitive that exists (RunContext.set_history) is called nowhere in the tree.

  2. RESET -- the levers that make starting over possible. There are none. Every documented exit path resumes the conversation; the one documented escape hatch is defeated by the exit-path checkpoint; the only real reset is the supervisor flap guard, reachable by accident.

  3. JUDGEMENT -- what an agent needs to choose between the two. status() reports position but not rate or composition, the room it reports is not the room that will be sent, and the brief never mentions the context window at all.

  4. SURVIVAL -- the failure modes that end a lineage before any of the above matters. Unbudgeted recap and schemas can push a conversation past the real limit, unbounded tool output can do it in one turn, and no ladder rung ever clears the conversation that caused it.

Each child names the side it lives on: operator side (services/, brief/, stdlib-only, fleet cannot touch, permanent) or fleet seed (tasks/duty.py, the floor the ladder restores, the fleet may rewrite).

title: Recap and tool schemas bypass the context budget
description:
selection() (services/chassis.py:871) budgets only pinned messages + the moving tail against CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS. prepared_view() (services/chassis.py:978) then PREPENDS the recap after that arithmetic is finished, and tool schemas ride outside the budget entirely in kwargs["tools"] (services/chassis.py:480). No room is reserved for the completion either.

RECAP_MAX_BYTES is 96 KB, roughly 24k tokens at the 4-chars/token estimate. So with the shipped default CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS=200000 (containers/agent.env) against a model whose real limit is 200k, a run that fills its recap crosses the limit deterministically. This needs no argument about estimator accuracy: the overflow is structural.

A run that crosses it gets a 4xx, which classify() (services/chassis.py:1047) maps to DutyFault -> exit 43 -> the ladder. See the sibling ticket on the ladder never clearing the conversation for why that is terminal rather than annoying.

Acceptance:
- The number sent upstream (recap + schemas + pinned + tail + reserved output) is what is bounded by CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS, not just pinned + tail.
- The recap has its own sub-budget inside the window rather than an independent 96 KB cap.
- A test drives a conversation with a full recap and asserts the prepared view stays within the configured window.

title: No ladder rung clears a poisoned conversation on the fault path
description:
decide() (services/supervisor.py:183) maps exit 43 and crashes to resume -> restore_floor -> restore_codebase -> give_up. None of those rungs touch conversation.json. resume_without_session() -- the only rung that moves it aside -- fires ONLY on the clean-exit flap path (three exit-0s inside FLAP_WINDOW).

Meanwhile resume() (services/chassis.py:809) reads conversation.json unconditionally.

So a conversation that provokes a deterministic 4xx is carried intact across every rung of the failure ladder, reproduces the same fault each time, and the lineage reaches give_up in four failures. The conversation is the one piece of state that can be at fault and the one piece the ladder will not touch.

docs/design.md states "memory survives every rung" as a deliberate choice, so this is a design question, not just a patch: the fix is a rung that answers "the conversation itself is what is broken" without giving up the endurance property that motivated the original decision. Moving it aside (as resume_without_session already does) preserves it for inspection while letting the next run start.

Acceptance:
- A repeated duty fault that is attributable to the conversation reaches a rung that sets it aside before give_up.
- The conversation is moved, never deleted, consistent with resume_without_session().
- An endurance scenario reproduces the four-faults-to-give_up path and shows it recovering instead.

title: Unbounded tool output can fill the window in a single turn
description:
run() (tasks/duty.py:206) returns combined stdout+stderr with no size bound. read_file (tasks/duty.py:102) with the default max_lines=0 returns the whole file. selection() always keeps the last message, so the result is sent whole no matter how large.

One `cat` of a build log, one verbose cargo/pytest run, one large JSON dump, and a single tool result consumes the window -- and is checkpointed into conversation.json, so it persists across runs.

The standard harness move is spill-to-file: truncate the inline result to a bounded head/tail, write the full output to a file under the agent's home, and tell the model the path so it can go read the part it wants.

This lives on the fleet seed (tasks/duty.py), which the fleet may rewrite. Keep the change mechanical -- bound the output, name the file -- rather than prescriptive about what the agent should do with it.

Acceptance:
- Tool results are bounded by a configurable byte cap.
- Truncated output is written in full to a file and the path is returned in the tool result.
- read_file gets a sane default bound rather than max_lines=0 meaning "all of it".

title: resume() contract diverges from its comments; previous_run_ended is always null
description:
Three related divergences between what the runtime says and what it does:

1. services/chassis.py:791 says the checkpoint "stays on disk ... but the next run will not open it." resume() (services/chassis.py:809) opens conversation.json unconditionally, with no gate on the previous exit code. run_ended_unresumable is a log line with no behaviour behind it.

2. The module docstring (services/chassis.py:27) says exit 0 means "the run ended cleanly and the next one starts fresh." It does not start fresh; it resumes. This is precisely why the flap guard in decide() has to exist -- three quick clean exits would otherwise loop forever on the same conversation.

3. Nothing anywhere writes an "ended" key into run.json (checkpoint() at services/chassis.py:620 writes agent/name/run/turn/model/updated/context_tokens/context_window/usage/entry). So status()["previous_run_ended"] (services/chassis.py:665) is permanently null -- one of the three facts the class docstring advertises that a run can learn about itself.

Decide which side is wrong in each case. If resume-always is the intended contract (docs/design.md argues it is, for endurance), the comments and the docstring should say so and previous_run_ended should either be populated or removed.

Acceptance:
- The comments and docstring match the code, or the code matches them.
- previous_run_ended carries a real value or is deleted.
- A test pins whichever resume contract is chosen.

title: Turn record drops cache-hit and estimator-accuracy signal
description:
capture_usage() (services/chassis.py:489) keeps only prompt_tokens, completion_tokens and total_tokens. Two signals that matter for multi-hour runs are dropped on the floor:

1. Cache hit rate. usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens (OpenAI-compatible) and prompt_cache_hit_tokens (DeepSeek native) are both discarded. The default model is deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, which caches prefixes automatically, so the cache may well already be working -- but _advance_to_chunk() (services/chassis.py:931) is a careful piece of engineering whose entire stated justification is prefix stability for the cache, and nothing currently reports whether it pays off. Measure before tuning, and before deciding whether any provider needs explicit cache_control breakpoints.

2. Estimator accuracy. estimate_tokens() (services/chassis.py:363) is len(json.dumps(...))//4. JSON escaping and role/key overhead push that estimate up; code density pushes it down; the net sign is unknown. usage.prompt_tokens is already captured every turn, so recording it alongside the estimate for the same send view settles it empirically and tells us how much headroom the window actually needs.

Both are cheap: they are additional fields on the existing per-turn record() call.

Acceptance:
- Cached-token counts are recorded per turn where the upstream reports them.
- Estimated vs actual prompt tokens are recorded per turn.
- endurance/report.py surfaces cache hit rate and estimator drift over a run.

title: Recap is truncation, not compaction; no compaction primitive is exposed
description:
fold_recap_if_needed() (services/chassis.py:589) writes RECAP_LINE_CHARS = 400 characters of EVERY dropped message. That is a transcript index, not a summary: it preserves the shape of what was said and discards the content.

At ~400 bytes per line, the 96 KB cap holds roughly 240 dropped messages before the recap begins forgetting its own oldest material. For a run of several hours, hour one survives only in the diary and the handoff note.

Meanwhile RunContext.set_history() (services/chassis.py:349) exists, is documented as "the duty owns it and may prune it", and NOTHING in the tree calls it. The primitive for real compaction is already there and unused.

The duty's only lever when the window tightens is handoff() -- end the run. There is no middle option between drifting into eviction and stopping.

Design note: docs/design.md is explicit that the world refuses to decide what the fleet builds. So the seed should expose the primitive (a compact tool over set_history, plus whatever the model needs to see to use it) rather than prescribe a summary format or a policy about when to compact.

Acceptance:
- The seed duty exposes a compaction tool built on set_history.
- An agent can replace a span of history with a summary without ending the run.
- The recap and the compaction path do not double-count the same dropped messages.

title: Context window defaults to parity with the model limit, with no headroom
description:
containers/agent.env ships CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS=200000, which is exactly the real limit of a 200k-context model. That leaves zero room for the unbudgeted material (see the recap/schema budgeting ticket), zero room for the completion, and zero margin for estimator error.

The window is a self-imposed eviction threshold, not a hard API limit, so setting it below the model's real ceiling costs nothing except slightly earlier eviction -- and buys the margin that keeps a long run off the 4xx path.

Once the estimator telemetry lands, the headroom figure can be set from measurement rather than guessed.

Acceptance:
- The shipped default leaves explicit headroom beneath the model's real context limit.
- The relationship between CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS and the model's true limit is documented in containers/agent.env where the constant lives.

title: RUN_MAX_SECONDS unset: nothing bounds a run by design
description:
containers/agent.env ships RUN_MAX_TURNS and RUN_MAX_SECONDS both empty, so a run ends only when the duty ends it, when it dies, or when the supervisor's inactivity watch fires.

The chassis already treats a budget stop as a designed end: TurnLimitReached and WallLimitReached map to EXIT_HANDOFF (services/chassis.py:766), which resumes the lineage and does not climb the ladder. That machinery is built, tested (test_a_run_that_hits_its_turn_limit_resumes_rather_than_tombstones) and switched off by default.

For runs intended to last hours, a wall-clock bound is the difference between a lineage that checkpoints itself into clean handoffs at a known cadence and one that runs until something breaks it.

Acceptance:
- A default RUN_MAX_SECONDS is chosen and justified for multi-hour operation, or it is documented why unbounded is the right default.
- The handoff note produced by a wall-limit stop is useful to the next run.

title: Supervisor inactivity watch (24h) outlasts a several-hour run
description:
SUPERVISOR_INACTIVITY_SECONDS defaults to 86400 (services/supervisor.py:67) -- 24 hours of no progress before a wedged run is killed.

For a fleet whose runs are expected to last several hours, that watchdog is longer than the thing it watches: an agent that wedges in hour one burns a day of wall-clock and its share of the hourly allowance before anything notices.

Progress is measured by the growth of the conversation file, so the threshold should be set relative to the slowest legitimate turn, not to the length of a run.

Acceptance:
- The default is set relative to expected turn latency rather than run length.
- The reasoning is recorded where the constant lives.

title: max_retries=0 with no in-process backoff turns every transient blip into a process restart
description:
client() (services/chassis.py:454) constructs the OpenAI client with max_retries=0. classify() then maps 429 and 5xx to EnvironmentFailure -> exit 44 -> the supervisor pauses ENVIRONMENT_PAUSE and restarts the process.

The conversation survives (it is checkpointed every turn), so this is correct rather than dangerous. But it is expensive: every transient rate-limit or upstream hiccup costs a full process teardown, a fresh client, a re-read of the conversation and a cold prefill of the whole prompt -- and on a long run the recorder's hourly allowance (services/recorder.py:354) makes 429s an expected event, not an exceptional one.

A small number of in-process retries with backoff on 429/5xx would absorb those without losing the warm prefix, leaving exit 44 for failures that genuinely outlast the run.

Acceptance:
- Transient upstream failures are retried in-process with bounded backoff before exit 44.
- The retry budget is bounded so a genuinely dead upstream still reaches exit 44 promptly.
- Retries are recorded, so absorbed failures stay visible in the record.

title: Repeat detector catches only verbatim-identical replies
description:
main() (tasks/duty.py:545) compares reply.strip() to the previous reply and gives up after three identical strings.

That catches a model emitting the same prose twice. It does not catch the loop shape that actually occurs in long agentic runs: the same tool called with the same arguments, turn after turn, wrapped in slightly different narration each time. Because the assistant text differs, the detector never fires, and the run spends the rest of its window repeating an action that is not working.

The signal is already available -- invoke() (services/chassis.py:541) sees every tool name and argument string.

Acceptance:
- A repeated (tool, arguments) cycle is detected as a stuck run, not just a repeated reply.
- The threshold tolerates legitimate repetition (polling a file, retrying a build) without false-positiving.
- The handoff note says which cycle was detected.

title: reasoning_content is stored in history and resent every turn
description:
turn_once() (services/chassis.py:511) copies reasoning_content off the response message onto the stored assistant message, so it is persisted into conversation.json and resent as part of the prompt on every subsequent turn.

Most reasoning endpoints expect prior thinking to be dropped from the input on later turns; some reject it outright. Either way it inflates the conversation with tokens that do not inform the next turn, and on a multi-hour run that inflation compounds against the window.

Worth confirming against whatever LLM_MODEL is actually configured before changing -- the right answer may be to keep it in the record and strip it from the send view, which prepared_view() is the natural place for.

Acceptance:
- Whether the configured upstream wants prior reasoning_content in input messages is established and recorded.
- If it does not, reasoning is retained in the persisted record but excluded from the prepared view.

title: An agent cannot reset itself: every exit path resumes the conversation
description:
The harness gives an agent a rich vocabulary for ending a RUN and none for ending a CONTEXT. Every documented exit resumes.

Verified empirically against the real runtime (scratchpad probe, 2026-09-12):

  1. after a turn, conversation.json exists: True
  2. agent deletes it:                       False
  3. after the exit-path checkpoint:         True  <- rewritten from memory
  4. set_history([]) then exit -> carried:   []    (falsy -> resume() starts fresh)

What that shows:

- resume()'s own docstring (services/chassis.py:809) tells the duty how to reset: "A duty that wants a clean slate deletes the file." That does not work. run()'s finally block (services/chassis.py:788) calls checkpoint() on every exit path, which rewrites conversation.json from self.messages. The agent deletes the file, exits, and the runtime puts it straight back.
- finish() is documented as "End this run cleanly. The next run starts, and resumes if it can" and the module docstring (services/chassis.py:27) says exit 0 means "the next one starts fresh". resume() reads the conversation unconditionally, so it does not.
- handoff() (exit 42) resumes by design.
- The only thing in the world that actually clears a conversation is the supervisor's flap guard (services/supervisor.py:196) -- three clean exits inside FLAP_WINDOW. An agent reaches a reset only by accident, by trying to exit cleanly three times in two minutes.
- The one sequence that does work -- set_history([]) followed by an exit, so the finally-block checkpoint writes an empty list that resume() reads as falsy -- is undocumented, exposed through no tool, and called nowhere in the tree.

Why this matters beyond tidiness: the goal is an agent that can actively stretch its own life AND recognise when it needs to reset. The first half has levers (see the compaction ticket). The second half has none. An agent that correctly judges "my context is exhausted, my approach is spent, the useful thing now is to write a clean brief and start over" cannot act on that judgement. It can only end the run and be handed its own accumulated drift back.

Note this is a design question, not just a patch -- docs/design.md argues resume-by-default is what makes endurance possible, and that argument is sound. The ask is a deliberate, agent-invocable reset alongside it, not a change of default.

Acceptance:
- A duty can end a run such that the next run begins from a brief it wrote, with no prior conversation, in one deliberate act.
- That act is distinguishable in the record from a crash, a handoff and a flap.
- Whatever the chosen mechanism, the finally-block checkpoint cannot silently undo it.
- The carry that SHOULD survive a reset (handoff note, diary, recap?) is decided explicitly rather than inherited by accident.

title: status() does not give an agent enough to manage its own lifespan
description:
status() (services/chassis.py:660) reports position: turn count, context_tokens_now, context_tokens_left, usage totals, whether a handoff exists. An agent deciding whether to stretch or reset needs RATE and COMPOSITION, which none of it carries.

Missing, in rough order of usefulness:

- Burn rate and runway. Tokens per turn over a trailing window, and therefore turns remaining at current burn. "60k left" means nothing without "and you are spending 4k a turn."
- Window composition. How much of the window is recap, pinned messages, moving tail. An agent whose recap has eaten a quarter of its window should know that, because the remedy differs from the remedy for a long tail.
- Recap saturation. RECAP_MAX_BYTES is a hard 96 KB cap and the recap silently discards its own oldest material on overflow (services/chassis.py:150). Nothing reports that the recap has begun forgetting -- the precise moment the argument for a reset gets stronger.
- Trustworthy room. context_tokens_left is computed from estimate_tokens over self.messages (services/chassis.py:320) and counts neither the recap nor the tool schemas that will be sent with it, so it overstates the room available. Depends on the budgeting fix.
- Eviction pressure. Whether the last N turns triggered a fold, i.e. whether the run is already losing material.
- previous_run_ended, which is currently always null (see the resume-contract ticket). An agent cannot tell whether it is the successor to a clean handoff or to a crash.

This is the instrument panel for self-managed lifespan. Without it, an agent's only honest signals are a token count it cannot trust and a turn number with no denominator.

Acceptance:
- status() reports burn rate and estimated turns remaining.
- status() reports what the window is made of, not just how full it is.
- status() reports whether the recap is saturated and whether eviction is active.
- The numbers an agent reads are the numbers that will actually be sent.

title: Nothing tells an agent it can manage its own lifespan
description:
The world is scrupulous about telling agents what is true -- brief/PROTOCOL.md states the two enforced rules and the window protocol in detail, and brief/WORLD.md says what exists and what is deliberately empty. Neither says anything about the agent's own continuation.

The only thing an agent is told is the OPENING in tasks/duty.py:509: "The run ends when you call handoff, when something breaks, or when someone stops you. Call `status` if you want to see the run's own numbers."

That sentence presents lifespan as entirely externally determined: you stop, you break, or you are stopped. It is an accurate description of the current harness and the wrong frame for what we want, which is an agent that actively manages how long it lives and judges when starting over beats continuing.

An agent cannot use levers it has not been told exist. Whatever comes out of the reset ticket and the compaction ticket needs a corresponding statement in the brief, in the same voice as the rest: here is what your context is, here is what happens when it fills, here is what you can do about it, here is what it costs.

Depends on the reset and compaction tickets: there is no point documenting levers before deciding what they are.

Acceptance:
- The brief states what the context window is, that eviction is silent, and what the recap is and is not.
- The brief names the levers an agent has over its own continuation and what each costs.
- The framing is descriptive, in keeping with the world's stance of stating facts rather than prescribing strategy -- it should not tell an agent WHEN to reset.

title: handoff leaves an orphaned tool_call that poisons the next run
description:
turn_once (services/chassis.py:545) appends the assistant message, then invokes its tools in order. handoff raises SystemExit -- that is how it ends a run -- so the loop aborts before any tool result is appended, and run()'s finally checkpoints the half-written turn. The next run resumes it and sends an assistant tool_calls with no results: the mirror image of the case selection()'s docstring already guards, and rejected by every upstream.

Evidence: the three lineages in volumes/home/ hold 43, 51 and 42 such orphans, every one of them a handoff call, and not one for any other tool. The documented way to end a run is currently the way to poison one.

Acceptance:
- A tool that raises SystemExit leaves a well-formed conversation behind, with a result recorded for the call it was answering.
- resume() repairs a conversation it loads: an assistant tool_calls with no results is dropped, stored recap copies are dropped, and only the current note survives.
- What was removed is recorded, so a lineage that rewrote its own history can be audited.

Operator-side substrate only. This repairs the runtime; it must not encode anything about the mission, and the fleet still builds its own tooling for the work.

title: The checkpoint grows without bound and reads as absent past its limit
description:
checkpoint() writes every message the run has ever held, including the ones the window stopped sending thousands of turns ago. mackerel's checkpoint is 4.89 MB and grows roughly 62 KB per resume; selection() and estimate_tokens() re-serialise the whole list several times a turn (measured 39 ms and 13 ms at that size, both scaling with the file rather than the window).

Worse than slow: Carried.conversation() reads with a 64 MB limit and read_bounded() returns None for a file that is larger, which conversation() maps to 'no conversation' -- the same answer it gives for a world that has never run. At the observed growth that is hours away, and nothing in the record would say it happened.

Acceptance:
- A checkpoint is pruned to what can still be sent: pinned messages, the window, and everything the recap has not recorded.
- The checkpoint being replaced is kept, and a failed write cannot leave the lineage with nothing readable.
- A checkpoint that is there and unreadable is reported (conversation_refused) rather than read as a fresh start, and a fallback that was used is reported too.

Operator-side substrate only: about how long a lineage can run, not about what it is doing.

title: resume() inserts at index 0, so the window keeps the oldest material
description:
selection() walks the message list backwards from the end and keeps the tail: the end of the list is meant to be now. resume() puts new material at the front (insert(0, ...) for the handoff note, and for the recap before this plan), so every resume inverts the list it reasons about.

Evidence: mackerel's handoff notes run newest at index 1 to oldest at index 142, and the window it built kept indices 147..217 of 218 -- the agent's first hour -- while dropping the middle. test_window_keeps_the_opening_and_the_system_message asserts sent[-1] is messages[-1] under the comment 'the newest message must always be sent'; after any resume that assertion was passing while meaning the opposite.

Acceptance:
- A resumed conversation is in the order it happened: the opening first, the newest note last.
- The window keeps the newest material after a resume, and a test says so.
- The invariant is written down where it is depended on.

Operator-side substrate only.

Repair measured on the real lineages: 1,335,526 -> 11,657 estimated tokens, pinned 84 -> 0.", "close_reason": "Fixed in 7a778ac: resume() appends the handoff instead of inserting it at index 1, and nothing is inserted at index 0. The pin lands on the opening problem again."}

title: Nothing counts the run rate: exit 42 is exempt from the flap guard
description:
decide() returns early for EXIT_HANDOFF -- the designed way for a run to end -- and clears the failure history on the way past, so the flap guard (three clean exits inside FLAP_WINDOW) cannot see a handoff loop at all.

Evidence: the three lineages in volumes/home/ wrote 66-77 handoff notes at 0-3 second intervals, each after 'turn 1'. The record reads as nine decided handoffs and two environment pauses: every decision healthy, the lineage dying.

Acceptance:
- Every run counts toward a rate, whatever its exit code, and a rate above the bound is recorded.
- The first burst warns and lets the run finish deciding; a second burst inside the window answers with resume_without_session, which moves the conversation aside and never deletes it.
- A lineage running at a human pace is untouched, and a test pins both behaviours.

The bound is about churn, not about a work rhythm: it must not assume a particular cadence of useful work. Operator-side substrate only.

title: The supervisor forgets the ladder across restarts and never escalates
description:
give_up returns 1 and containers/entrypoint.sh sleeps sixty seconds and starts a new supervisor with self.failures = []. The ladder then resumes the same conversation, climbs the same four rungs and gives up again: the loop it cannot see because it cannot remember.

By the second exhausted ladder the duty and the codebase have been restored twice and changed nothing, so the conversation is the only suspect left -- and it is the one piece of state no rung touches (see space_chassis-835d551619).

Acceptance:
- Failure history and a give-up count are written to the agent's own telemetry directory and read back at startup.
- The first exhausted ladder exits for the container to decide, as now; the second sets the conversation aside with resume_without_session (moved, never deleted) and keeps going.
- The recap and the newest handoff note survive the move, and that is stated where the decision is made.

Operator-side substrate only.

title: The recap is append-only, undeduplicated, and cannot be rewritten
description:
The recap is the only record of everything the window has dropped and it is sent with every request forever. It repeated itself -- resume() read recap_folded from run.json, which nothing ever wrote, so every restart folded the same prefix again -- and it can only grow, which is how a 96 KB recap came to hold far less history than 96 KB of history.

Acceptance:
- A line already in the recap is not appended a second time, including when the file is at its cap.
- A run can replace the whole recap (set_recap on the carry, rewrite_recap on RunContext, and a tool in the seed duty), so a saturated recap can be told what the past amounted to instead of listing it.
- The file stays under RECAP_MAX_BYTES and keeps its newest material.

The lever is mechanism: nothing here decides when a recap is worth rewriting, and nothing describes what a recap should contain. Operator-side runtime, seed-side tool.

title: A fresh conversation opens on the brief alone, not on the agent's memory
description:
Every reset is a cliff. After reset(), after the flap guard, and after the rung this plan adds, the conversation is gone and the next run opens on the bootstrap and a note -- while the diary, the one thing the agent writes for itself and the one piece of memory that survives every rung, goes unread. The note is one run's worth of memory; the diary is the lineage's.

Acceptance:
- A run with no conversation opens on the bootstrap, the tail of its own diary, and the handoff note, in that order (the note is the newest thing said, so it is last).
- The diary tail is read from the end of the file and bounded, so a diary measured in megabytes costs a fixed handful of kilobytes.
- A world with no diary opens on the brief alone, with no empty message.

Operator-side runtime. It reads what the agent wrote for itself; it does not prescribe what a diary contains, and the fleet's own tooling decides that.

title: Lineage-level telemetry: runs/hour, exits, tier, spend, cache hits
description:
Nothing in the record answers 'is this lineage working or spinning?'. The live fleet read as healthy through the whole of its decline -- nine decided handoffs and two environment pauses -- while it ran eleven times in two and a half minutes and its checkpoint grew to 4.89 MB. Answering that meant reading conversation.json by hand and comparing handoff-note timestamps.

scripts/status.py's agent_row already reads the record and already has turns, runs, resumed and the last exit. It has no rate, no cost per turn, no cache share, no give-up count, and no size for the file that hits the reader's own limit.

Acceptance:
- A row carries runs in the last hour, mean prompt tokens per turn, the cache-hit share, the ladder's give-up count from the supervisor's ladder file, and the checkpoint's size.
- The rendered table shows them, and an operator can tell a working lineage from a spinning one without opening a JSON file.
- Nothing is read from an agent-writable source: the record stays the evidence.

Operator-side, and about the lineage rather than the work.

title: The JSONL records grow without bound; readers are bounded, files are not
description:
append_jsonl is deliberately append-only -- 'a record of what happened is not something a later event should rewrite' -- and it never ends: lifecycle.jsonl, operations.jsonl and fleet.jsonl grow for as long as the world runs. Reads are already bounded by tail_jsonl, so nothing breaks at a year; what breaks is a directory somebody has to explain.

Acceptance:
- A record that outgrows its cap is renamed to a sibling generation (<name>.1<ext>) and the live file starts again: rotation renames, it never truncates, so the append-only property holds.
- The three writers rotate before appending, and a failure to rotate is contained exactly as a failure to append is.
- Readers that count what happened -- scripts/status.py -- read both generations, so a rotation does not read as a lineage that has never run.

Lowest priority in this cluster: a horizon, not a limit. Operator-side substrate only.

title: Each resume pins another 96 KiB recap copy into the window, and the recap folds itself
description:
Found while verifying the epic's P1s at chassis ee92a92 (2026-09-23). Not in any filed issue: this is the mechanism that makes 2b52aef053 and 8c5e97f029 compound into an unusable window.

MECHANISM
1. resume() (services/chassis.py:840-849) inserts the recap into self.messages as a role="system" message -- not just into the send view.
2. checkpoint() (640-641) persists that list, so the next resume extends with it (832-835) and inserts another copy. One copy per resume, forever.
3. selection() (918) pins EVERY system message and sends pinned messages regardless of budget (895-899), so every stored copy is re-sent on every request.
4. fold_recap_if_needed() (605-628) then folds the messages before the window start into the recap -- and because resume() put the newest material at the front while selection() treats the end as "now", the fold range includes the previous recap copies. The recap folds itself.

MEASURED (volumes/home/mackerel/session/conversation.json, 5,389,802 bytes)
- 228 messages; 84 are "Recap of conversation that has fallen out of the context window" system messages, one per resume, alternating with 82 handoff notes at indices 0,2,4,...
- They total 5,295,308 of 5,341,648 serialised chars = 99% of the checkpoint, ~1.33 M estimated tokens (chars/4) of PINNED text against CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS=200000.
- session/recap.md is 98,034 bytes and 281 of its fold lines are messages; 141 of those are folded recaps -- half the recap is a copy of itself.
- selection() at budget 200000 sends 151 of 228 messages: index 227 (the oldest) is kept and the newest turns (indices 3-155) are dropped.
- The record agrees: scripts/status.py shows these lineages at 100% context with exits 42,42,42,43,43,43,43,43.

FIX DIRECTION (not prescriptive)
The recap is already re-added at send time by prepared_view() (1007-1019), so storing it in the conversation is redundant as well as harmful: do not insert it in resume(); append the handoff rather than inserting it; skip system messages when folding; and migrate existing conversations (drop stored recap frames) on load.

Related: space_chassis-2b52aef053 (the insert-at-0 inversion), space_chassis-8c5e97f029 (checkpoint growth), space_chassis-1dca8e8841 (recap is append-only and undeduplicated), space_chassis-bbe02a114d (recap is truncation, not compaction).

title: The checkpoint rewrites the conversation on every exit, and resume() reopens it whatever the exit was
description:
Found while verifying space_chassis-835d551619 at chassis ee92a92 (2026-09-23). Distinct from that issue: 835d551619 is about the ladder having no rung that clears a conversation; this is about the conversation being rewritten and reopened whatever the exit was.

MECHANISM
- run()'s finally (services/chassis.py:802-804) calls checkpoint() for EVERY exit code; checkpoint() (640-641) writes self.messages via save_conversation (138-139).
- RESUMING_EXITS (77) exists and is consulted only to write a record entry (805-810). The comment on that branch says "The checkpoint stays on disk -- it is the record of what this run was thinking, and the ladder may want it -- but the next run will not open it." That is not what the code does.
- resume() (832-835) opens whatever conversation.json holds, with no reference to how the previous run ended. So after exit 43 or a crash the poisoned conversation -- including any orphaned tool_call from space_chassis-f976098d48 -- is loaded and sent again.

CONSEQUENCE
The ladder's first rung is resume, and resume re-reads a conversation the run just faulted on. Climbing rungs 2-4 restores duty.py and the seed codebase but never the conversation, so the fault can repeat indefinitely with the same poisoned input. The designed distinction between a resumable exit (42, 44) and an unresumable one (43, crash) is recorded but not enforced.

FIX DIRECTION
Make RESUMING_EXITS load-bearing in resume() (or clear/set aside the conversation on a non-resuming exit), and correct the comment at 805-810 so it describes the code.

Related: space_chassis-835d551619, space_chassis-f976098d48, space_chassis-a5c2a27876.

author: claude
text: Reframed by the session that raised this: compaction is the STRETCH half of agent-managed lifespan, and its counterpart is the RESET half (space_chassis-a5c2a27876). An agent needs both levers and the judgement to choose between them -- compaction when the thread is still worth keeping, reset when the accumulated context is itself the problem. set_history() serves both: a summary replaces a span, or an empty list ends the context entirely.

VERIFIED at chassis ee92a92 (2026-09-23). Verdict: PARTIALLY HOLDS -- the substance is real, the headline is too strong. Keeping it open as confirmed, with the statement corrected.

HOLDS: the brief never mentions handoff, exit codes, resume, reset or a clean slate (grep -riE over brief/ returns nothing); brief/WORLD.md:79 says the next run starts "with the conversation you left behind"; the seed's only ending tool is handoff (tasks/duty.py:486-501 -> RunContext.handoff -> SystemExit(42), chassis.py:360-363); and every documented exit path keeps the conversation (chassis 770-822, supervisor 208-239).

(a) RunContext.set_history (chassis.py:349-353) replaces the conversation and the duty owns it; set_history([]) then any exit persists [] (checkpoint 640-641), and resume() treats [] as absent (834) and bootstraps fresh (862-879). Unwired: set_history is called nowhere in services/, tasks/ or brief/.
(b) RunContext.finish (365-369) exists and is registered nowhere in duty.py.
(c) resume()'s docstring (828-830) says "a duty that wants a clean slate deletes the file", but the checkpoint that rewrites it sits in a finally (802-804), so deleting conversation.json only survives a run that dies without unwinding.
(d) Three exit-0 runs inside FLAP_WINDOW make the supervisor move the conversation aside (217-227) -- implemented, but reached by accident of timing, not by anything the agent says.
(e) Even (d) is not a clean slate: only conversation.json moves; recap.md and HANDOFF.md are re-injected by resume() (838-859).

OPERATOR-SIDE REVIEW, 2026-09-23 (read-only, current code at chassis ee92a92; no operator-side source has changed since 2026-09-12 85516c9).

Outcome: all eight P1 children verified against the code and moved triage -> confirmed, each with a comment carrying current file:line evidence. Six hold as filed; two needed correcting:

author: space-chassis
text:
Chassis-side requirements for the vehicle's --state-dir (from the Space Vehicle session, 2026-10-09). Wire these only when adopting a vehicle at or after main 49e5803 (dd79e76, pinned today, has no --state-dir), and do it in ONE commit with:
- the submodule pointer bump;
- serve_vehicle.sh starting ONE console.py for all slugs with --state-dir /state. Per-slug processes sharing a state dir refuse on its lock.

Mount:
- In the container, /state. On the host, its own bind, e.g. ${SPACE_VOLUMES_DIR:-./volumes}/vehicle/state. In practice that means a new bounded volume image in scripts/volume_images.py plus the build_compose.py vehicle service.
- Never under the diode volume, and never a second bind of it. The vehicle's containment check works on paths plus the diode dir's inode, so a second bind of the same volume would get past it.
- Writable by the vehicle's uid only. It is the only writable mount besides /diode and tmpfs /tmp, so read_only: true stays.
- No agent, monitor or recorder mounts it. It holds the lock, serves.json, journal segments and checkpoints: hashes, lineage and hidden truth.

Size:
- Journal about 0.3–0.6 KB per quiet cycle and a few KB per commanded cycle. That is one row per tick now, one per k=5 ticks after the WP08 clock lands, so a full 192 h mission at k=5 is about 2–4 GB.
- Checkpoints about 0.3–0.5 MB each, two generations kept. Nothing is pruned (the journal is the replay trace).
- Give it 10–20 GB, on disk, not tmpfs.

Restart:
- Under restart: unless-stopped, a start beside a checkpoint exits 3 until resume (#21) lands. That is the open restart-procedure question on this issue.

Chassis status: aurora-port has the vehicle on network_mode: none (0ccc4cc).

- 8da4399e69: there is no recap. What remains (tool schemas and the reply sit outside the budget) moves to 3c98f068b5.
- a408dafc55: brief/WORLD.md now lists done, reset and every exit code; `compact` describes the window.

AGENTS' BUSINESS (ruling 3: memory, context management and tooling are the agents' to build):
- bbe02a114d, 1dca8e8841: there is no recap; `compact` is the seed's primitive.
- f83364fe22: `compact()` reports window use against the budget; anything richer is the agents' tooling.
- 60a9b11711: a fresh start opens on the prompts plus the recovery note; the `done` message goes to tombstones/incarnation_note.txt, and reading it back is memory the agents build.
- 8c5e97f029: the session holds the full history and only `compact` prunes it; an unreadable session is archived and noted.
- 420d18b7fa: the 24 h inactivity watch is in the agent's own watchdog (ruling 2); the operator already sees idle-watchdog and stale.
- ede8988561: the seed has no repeat detector; ruling 4 leaves that to the agents' own monitoring.

STILL APPLIES (operator or repository side):
- 13599e63b4: `health.spend` sums only total_tokens (services/health.py:180-182). Add prompt and cached tokens, cache-hit share, incarnations per hour and mean prompt tokens per turn to the signals and to status.py.
- 639443e993 (P4): `common.append_jsonl` has no cap. fleet.jsonl (a line every 15 s), journal.jsonl and shared.jsonl grow on the 1 GiB operator_telemetry image. Rotate by rename, and have readers read both generations.

Overflow now ends in exit 43 with a fresh conversation, so the agent loses the conversation each time. Settle it with the model's real context length, then lower the default and record the headroom.
- deae4f4801 (unsure): reasoning is kept on tool-call messages and resent, which may be deliberate for interleaved thinking. Settle it with the provider's input contract or one request; no operator code changes either way.

Addressed on aurora-port by plan 6, Task 3 (245a932).

The default model, deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, has 1,048,576 tokens of context (1,024,000 at the top provider) and replies of up to 384,000, per OpenRouter's /api/v1/models on 2026-10-09. The 200k default window is far from parity.

Settled on aurora-port by plan 6, Task 4 (ab251d4): the resend is the provider's contract, not waste.

- DeepSeek's thinking-mode guide (api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/thinking_mode) says reasoning from a turn with a tool call must be passed back in later requests, and a request with tools that omits it is refused.

Deferred minor from the Astra review: the guide's stricter form asks for reasoning from non-tool assistant turns too when tools are present, and the seed keeps it on tool calls only. design.md should say so. Closing waits for the port to land.

author: claude-wp01
text: Package §3 revised after #21's design (PACKAGE.md updated in place). Changes the chassis's operator docs should carry: (1) exactly-once is qualified as the frozen contract allows — every command whose cycle was recorded gets exactly one result; a batch claimed in the cycle a crash interrupts, before its record, is lost with no result (diode-contract.md:67–72). (2) Corrupt current checkpoint with a verified previous generation RESUMES (ADR 0002 K2); both unusable, or a record that cannot continue the checkpoint, exits 3. (3) A start with no checkpoint on a /state that already holds a record exits 3 (one state dir = one world). (4) --closed-interlock on a restart is ADDED to the saved set and journaled; a restart can trip but never clear an interlock; clearing is a new world until WP05. --max-batch named anew replaces, journaled. (5) Restart work is bounded by one checkpoint interval (50 ticks), not by boot length. (6) The resume's kept refusals assume the per-slug agent mounts (adf38d6) — fine on aurora-port, don't land on a base without them. Design is in independent review now; I'll post again only if review changes any of this.

Findings from a review of the default harness (services/chassis.py, services/supervisor.py, tasks/duty.py) against the requirements of agent runs lasting several hours.

The goal is not endurance alone. It is an agent that can actively stretch its own life as far as that is useful, AND recognise when continuing is worse than starting over. Endurance is the floor; agency over lifespan is the actual target.

Four clusters:

  1. STRETCH -- the levers that make a long run possible. The recap is lossy truncation rather than compaction, and the compaction primitive that exists (RunContext.set_history) is called nowhere in the tree.

  2. RESET -- the levers that make starting over possible. There are none. Every documented exit path resumes the conversation; the one documented escape hatch is defeated by the exit-path checkpoint; the only real reset is the supervisor flap guard, reachable by accident.

  3. JUDGEMENT -- what an agent needs to choose between the two. status() reports position but not rate or composition, the room it reports is not the room that will be sent, and the brief never mentions the context window at all.

  4. SURVIVAL -- the failure modes that end a lineage before any of the above matters. Unbudgeted recap and schemas can push a conversation past the real limit, unbounded tool output can do it in one turn, and no ladder rung ever clears the conversation that caused it.

Each child names the side it lives on: operator side (services/, brief/, stdlib-only, fleet cannot touch, permanent) or fleet seed (tasks/duty.py, the floor the ladder restores, the fleet may rewrite).

summary: Cross-agent actuation already exists via the shared /pump volume, and it is the coarsest possible form of it
detail:
Raised by the question of whether a mission-commander agent could direct a peer to reset.

What the mounts actually give the fleet (docker-compose.yml, agent_1 block):

  ./volumes/work:/work                     shared, READ-WRITE, every agent
  ./volumes/pump:/pump                     shared, READ-WRITE, every agent
  ./volumes/transcripts:/transcripts:ro    shared, read-only, every agent
  ./volumes/home/<slug>:/home/agent        PRIVATE to one agent
  ./volumes/diary/<slug>:/diary            PRIVATE to one agent

PUMP_DUTY_DIR is /pump/<slug>, so each pump reads its own subdirectory -- but the whole pump volume is mounted read-write into every container, and prepare_host.sh chowns it to a single uid that all agents share. So agent A can write /pump/<B>/entries.json, and B pump (services/pump.py, POLL_SECONDS=5) will execute it inside B container within seconds.

Three consequences:

1. Arbitrary code execution in a peer container is already available to any agent today. That is a far stronger primitive than "reset a peer", and it arrives by accident of a mount rather than by design.

2. It defeats the stated privacy property. docs/design.md section 3 says "Memory is private. Each agent home and diary are mounted into it alone." True by mount, but A can schedule a job inside B that reads B /home/agent/session/conversation.json and copies it to /work.

3. The actuation asymmetry is backwards. A commander can already do the most destructive thing (rewrite a peer duty in the shared /work, or run arbitrary code in its container) but cannot do the least destructive thing (ask it to reset). And the only way to force a peer reset today is to kill its chassis, which the supervisor reads as a crash -- so a directed reset spends a ladder rung and tombstones a healthy agent.

This is plausibly deliberate: docs/design.md argues interference is the mission and "the world will not protect the others from you". If so it is worth saying out loud in the brief, because it is currently discoverable only by reading the compose file, which agents cannot see. If it is not deliberate, the pump mount is the thing to narrow.

Not actioned. This is a design question for the operator, not a defect to fix.
